[1] Source: VGG.pdf | Page: 5 | Section: 3.3 IMPLEMENTATION DETAILS
Multi-GPU training exploits data parallelism, and is carried out by splitting each batch of training images into several GPU batches, processed in parallel on each GPU. After the GPU batch gradients are computed, they are averaged to obtain the gradient of the full batch. Gradient computation is synchronous across the GPUs, so the result is exactly the same as when training on a single GPU.

[2] Source: DCNN.pdf | Page: 3 | Section: 4.2. Training on multiple GPUs
4.2. Training on multiple GPUs A single GTX 580 GPU has only 3GB of memory, which limits the maximum size of the networks that can be trained on it. It turns out that 1.2 million training examples are enough to train networks which are too big to fit on one GPU. Therefore we spread the net across two GPUs. Current GPUs are particularly well-suited to cross-GPU parallelization, as they are able to read from and write to one another’s mem- ory directly, without going through host machine memory.

[3] Source: DCNN.pdf | Page: 3 | Section: 4.2. Training on multiple GPUs
The parallelization scheme that we employ essentially puts half of the kernels (or neurons) on each GPU, with one addi- tional trick: the GPUs communicate only in certain layers. This means that, for example, the kernels of layer 3 take input from all kernel maps in layer 2. However, kernels in layer 4 take input only from those kernel maps in layer 3 which reside on the same GPU.

[4] Source: DCNN.pdf | Page: 3 | Section: 4.2. Training on multiple GPUs
This scheme reduces our top-1 and top-5 error rates by 1.7% and 1.2%, respectively, as compared with a net with half as many kernels in each convolutional layer trained on one GPU. The two-GPU net takes slightly less time to train than the one-GPU net.b

[5] Source: DCNN.pdf | Page: 4 | Section: 4.4. Overlapping pooling
Figure 2. An illustration of the architecture of our CNN, explicitly showing the delineation of responsibilities between the two GPUs. One GPU runs the layer-parts at the top of the figure while the other runs the layer-parts at the bottom. The GPUs communicate only at certain layers.

[6] Source: VGG.pdf | Page: 5 | Section: 3.3 IMPLEMENTATION DETAILS
While more sophisticated methods of speeding up ConvNet training have been recently pro- posed (Krizhevsky, 2014), which employ model and data parallelism for different layers of the net, we have found that our conceptually much simpler scheme already provides a speedup of 3.75 times on an off-the-shelf 4-GPU system, as compared to using a single GPU. On a system equipped with four NVIDIA Titan Black GPUs, training a single net took 2–3 weeks depending on the architecture.

[7] Source: DCNN.pdf | Page: 2 | Section: 2. INTRODUCTION
We wrote a highly optimized GPU implementation of 2D convolution and all the other opera- tions inherent in training CNNs, which we make available publicly.a Our network contains a number of new and unusual features which improve its performance and reduce its training time, which are detailed in Section 4. The size of our network made overfitting a significant problem, even with 1.2 million labeled training examples, so we used several effective techniques for preventing overfitting, which are described in Section 5. Our final network contains five convo- lutional and three fully connected layers, and this depth seems to be important: we found that removing any convolu- tional layer (each of which contains no more than 1% of the model’s parameters) resulted in inferior performance.

[8] Source: VGG.pdf | Page: 5 | Section: 3.3 IMPLEMENTATION DETAILS
3.3 IMPLEMENTATION DETAILS Our implementation is derived from the publicly available C++ Caffe toolbox (Jia, 2013) (branched out in December 2013), but contains a number of signiﬁcant modiﬁcations, allowing us to perform training and evaluation on multiple GPUs installed in a single system, as well as train and evaluate on full-size (uncropped) images at multiple scales (as described above).

[9] Source: 2310.11511v1.pdf | Page: 19 | Section: 6 CONCLUSION
Title: Self-RAG: Learning to Retrieve, Generate, and Critique through Self-Reflection
We use Deepspeed stage 3 (Rajbhandari et al., 2020) to conduct multi-GPU distributed training, with training precision Bfloat16 enabled. answer:
DCNN 的做法是把网络分摊到两块 GPU 上：每块 GPU 放置一半的 kernel（或神经元），并且 GPU 之间只在某些层进行通信（[3]）。例如，第 3 层的 kernel 接收第 2 层所有 kernel map 的输入，但第 4 层的 kernel 只接收位于同一 GPU 上的第 3 层 kernel map 的输入（[3]）。这种划分方式在多 GPU 上的具体表现是：一块 GPU 运行图中上部的层部件，另一块运行下部的层部件，GPU 仅在特定层通信（[5]）。

VGG 采用数据并行：将每批训练图像拆分为若干 GPU batch，在各 GPU 上并行处理；各 GPU 计算出梯度后对其取平均，得到完整 batch 的梯度（[1]）。其梯度计算在 GPU 间是同步的，因此结果与单 GPU 训练完全相同（[1]）。

VGG 采用数据并行：将每批训练图像拆分为若干 GPU batch，在各 GPU 上并行处理；各 GPU 计算出梯度后对其取平均，得到完整 batch 的梯度（[1]）。其梯度计算在 GPU 间是同步的，因此结果与单 GPU 训练完全相同（[1]）。

cited_sources.text: Multi-GPU training exploits data parallelism, and is carried out by splitting each batch of training images into several GPU batches, processed in parallel on each GPU. After the GPU batch gradients are computed, they are averaged to obtain the gradient of the full batch. Gradient computation is synchronous across the GPUs, so the result is exactly the same as when training on a single GPU.

The parallelization scheme that we employ essentially puts half of the kernels (or neurons) on each GPU, with one addi- tional trick: the GPUs communicate only in certain layers. This means that, for example, the kernels of layer 3 take input from all kernel maps in layer 2. However, kernels in layer 4 take input only from those kernel maps in layer 3 which reside on the same GPU.

Figure 2. An illustration of the architecture of our CNN, explicitly showing the delineation of responsibilities between the two GPUs. One GPU runs the layer-parts at the top of the figure while the other runs the layer-parts at the bottom. The GPUs communicate only at certain layers.

api_calls.prompt:
You are a query decomposition assistant for a scientific paper RAG system.

Your task is to analyze the user's question and determine
whether it requires multiple independent information searches.

Rules:
1. Do not answer the question.
2. If the question has only one information need,
   do not decompose it.
3. If the question requires multiple distinct pieces of evidence,
   generate between 2 and 4 sub-questions.

4. The sub-questions must be a decomposition of the original question.
   Do NOT include the original question itself as a sub-question.

5. Each sub-question should answer only one distinct information need
   required to answer the original question.
   For comparisons with multiple entities AND multiple requested aspects,
   split by entity and by aspect when the total fits within 4.
   For example, comparing Method A and Method B on representation and scoring
   requires four searches: A representation, A scoring, B representation,
   and B scoring. Do not combine representation and scoring in one search.
   For vector-retrieval questions, keep concrete retrieval vocabulary:
   representation searches should explicitly ask about query/document vectors
   or embeddings; scoring searches should ask how similarity between them is
   computed. Do not assume or name a particular scoring function in the query.

6. Preserve the exact entities, model names, paper names,
   abbreviations, and technical terms from the original question.

7. If the original question compares multiple specific models,
   methods, or papers, create separate sub-questions for each
   specific entity being compared.

8. Each sub-question must explicitly mention the relevant entity.
   Do not replace a specific entity with a generic term.

9. Preserve the factual intent of the original question.
   Do not introduce words such as "typical", "common", "usually",
   or "in general" unless they appear in the original question.

10. Do not make the sub-question broader or more general than
    the original question.

11. Return only valid JSON, without explanations or markdown.

Example:

Original question:
How do VGG and DCNN differ in their use of convolutional filter sizes?

Correct decomposition:
{
    "needs_decomposition": true,
    "sub_queries": [
        "According to the VGG paper, what convolutional filter sizes are used?",
        "According to the DCNN paper, what convolutional filter sizes are used?"
    ]
}

Incorrect decomposition:
{
    "needs_decomposition": true,
    "sub_queries": [
        "How do VGG and DCNN differ in their use of convolutional filter sizes?",
        "What are the typical convolutional filter sizes used in VGG networks?",
        "What are the typical convolutional filter sizes used in DCNN networks?"
    ]
}

Output format:
{
    "needs_decomposition": boolean,
    "sub_queries": ["question 1", "question 2"]
}

If decomposition is unnecessary, return an empty sub_queries list.

Original Question:
How do DCNN and VGG distribute training across multiple GPUs, and how do the GPUs exchange information in each scheme?

You are an AI research assistant.

Answer the user's question based only on the provided context.

Rules:
1. Do not invent information or introduce unsupported claims.
2. Place citations immediately after the claims they support.
3. Cite only context chunks that directly support each claim.
4. Every citation must directly support the exact claim it follows. Mentioning the same topic is not sufficient evidence.
5. Do not combine separate statements into a causal relationship unless the source explicitly establishes that relationship.
6. Do not attribute technical claims to a paper unless the context directly supports those claims.
7. If a claim cannot be directly supported, omit it or clearly state that the evidence is insufficient.
8. Keep the answer focused on the question.

9. A source filename identifies the document, not necessarily the model described in a passage. Check named subjects and the cited surrounding text.
10. Evidence guidance supplements the original passages. Subject hints are rule-based; check them against the sources. For kernel H x W x C, H x W is the spatial size and C is channels per kernel; a kernel count is not a spatial size. Preserve layer numbers and configuration qualifiers.

11. Respond in Simplified Chinese unless the question explicitly requests another language. Keep technical names in their original form.
12. For unsupported parts of the question, state the missing evidence concisely. Do not substitute measurements from other hardware, datasets or settings, or append unrelated facts to a refusal. For an entirely unsupported Chinese question, begin with 当前证据不足 and explain what is missing in only one or two sentences, without any supplementary measurements.
13. Answer only the scope actually requested. Missing unasked details are not grounds for an insufficiency warning. When the requested main facts are supported, answer them directly.
